sources.title: NGSS MS-LS4-4: Construct an explanation based on evidence that describes how genetic variations of traits in a population increase some individuals' probability of surviving and reproducing in a specific environment

note.text: Peter and Rosemary Grant have studied the finches on one Galápagos island every year since 1976.
These two birds belong to the same species, the medium ground finch.
Beak size varies from bird to bird, and it's inherited: parents pass it to their young.
Some birds in the same population have thinner beaks.
Wide, deep beaks are good at cracking large, hard seeds.
Thinner beaks handle small, soft seeds well.

steps.title: A wet year
steps.question: An El Niño brought heavy rain: few large hard seeds, lots of small soft ones. Which birds did better?

options.feedback: Yes. They could eat the plentiful small seeds, so more of them survived and reproduced.
Their food, the large hard seeds, became scarce.
The food changed, so one beak type had an advantage.
Many survived, especially birds with beaks suited to the small seeds.

steps.title: The next generation
steps.question: In the years after the El Niño, what did the Grants find?

options.text: The average beak size in the population got smaller
options.feedback: Right. More thin-beaked parents meant more thin-beaked young. That's natural selection.

options.text: Each bird's beak shrank during its life
options.feedback: Individual birds don't change their beaks. The population changed over generations.
The small-beaked birds survived better, so the average got smaller.
The Grants measured a real change: the average beak got smaller.

steps.title: Natural selection
steps.instruction: Tap the steps of natural selection in order.
items: Birds with suited beaks survive and reproduce more
steps.why: Natural selection needs inherited variation. The environment decides which variations help survival.
steps.hint: It starts with differences that already exist.
